@graph.headline: What Is the 3-5-7 Rule in Trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 3-5-7 rule is a risk management framework with three caps: risk at most 3% of your account on any single trade, never more than 5% of your account at risk across all open trades, and aim for winners of roughly 7% — about 2.3 times the 3% risk. It is an informal, trader-created guideline, not a rule issued by any regulator or exchange, and it governs position sizing and exposure rather than telling you when to enter a trade.

mainEntity.name: What is the 3-5-7 rule in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 3-trade rule is not a standardized or universally accepted rule, so the term needs unpacking. Its most common meaning is the 3-strike rule: stop trading for the session after three consecutive losses, because three straight losses usually signal either a market out of sync with your system or an emotional state that will make the next trade worse. Some day traders also use it as a cap of three trades per day to control overtrading. Either way, it is a separate guardrail from 3-5-7, though the two pair well together.

The 3-5-7 rule itself sets no trade count — it caps risk, not frequency. As a practical guardrail, beginners should plan a maximum of three quality setups per day and take only those, because overtrading is one of the fastest ways to convert a good strategy into losses. Stop the session after three consecutive losses or when you hit your daily loss limit, whichever comes first. Fewer, planned trades beat many impulsive ones.

mainEntity.name: How many trades should I take per day?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 1% rule means risking no more than 1% of your account on any single trade — so a ₹1,00,000 account risks at most ₹1,000 per trade. It is more conservative than the 3-5-7 rule's 3%: ten straight losses at 1% compound to about a 9.6% drawdown, versus about 26.3% at 3%. Beginners should start with the 1% rule and graduate to 3% only after months of consistent, rule-following trading, not after one good week.

mainEntity.name: What is the 1% rule in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: A good risk-to-reward ratio is 2:1 or better — you aim to make at least twice what you risk. The 3-5-7 rule implies about 2.33:1, since a 7% target against a 3% risk is 2.33 times the risk, and at that ratio you only need a 30% win rate to break even before costs. Ratios below 1:1 demand a win rate above 50% just to survive, which is a hard way to trade. If a setup cannot realistically reach at least 2:1, skipping it is usually the correct decision.

Three straight losses mean either the market is against your system today or you are trading emotionally, and both are reasons to walk away rather than force a fourth trade. Note the distinction: three planned stop-outs within a valid strategy are normal statistics, while three emotional mistakes are a warning sign — but the action is the same either way, because the risk being managed is tilt, not bad luck. Review the trades the next day with a clear head.

mainEntity.name: Should I stop trading after three losses?

acceptedAnswer.text: Beginners manage risk with a short, non-negotiable routine: size every position from a fixed risk budget (start at 1% per trade), set the stop-loss before calculating size, keep total open risk under the 5% cap, set a daily loss limit and stop at it, log every trade, never average down into a losing position, and never take a revenge trade after a loss. Risk management is not one big decision — it is these small rules, applied on every trade without exception.
